Battle of Okinawa. The longest and costliest of the Pacific island campaigns, Okinawa from April to June nineteen forty-five saw American forces battle a Japanese garrison defending an island that would serve as a staging ground for the invasion of the Japanese home islands. With over one hundred thousand total casualties, the devastating battle reinforced American military planners' expectation that a direct invasion of Japan would be catastrophically expensive, a calculation that contributed to the decision to use atomic weapons.

The campaign lasted eighty-two days. The Japanese garrison of approximately seventy-seven thousand troops was commanded by General Masao Yoshida, while American forces, numbering approximately one hundred eighty-three thousand from Army, Navy, and Marine Corps, were under General Simon Buckner Jr. U.S. casualties reached seven thousand six hundred thirteen killed and thirty-one thousand wounded. Japanese casualties exceeded sixty-two thousand killed, with most refusing to surrender.

Japanese commanders also mobilized one hundred fifty thousand civilian conscripts as militia, and widespread civilian deaths are estimated at fifty thousand or more. The Japanese deployed massive kamikaze attacks that killed four thousand nine hundred seven U.S. Navy sailors and damaged numerous ships. Shuri Castle, the ancient seat of Okinawan royal power, became the centerpiece of Japanese defenses and was captured late in the campaign. Okinawa's strategic importance was clear—it was the final large island before the Japanese home islands and would serve as a necessary staging area for invasion operations. The anticipated losses for invasion of the home islands influenced American decision-makers' calculations on weapon alternatives.
